result:
A thousand words is enough for a small building. Not a cathedral — a shed, maybe, or one of those roadside fruit stands with a hand-painted sign and a coffee can for the honor system money. I've always liked those. They assume something about you before you arrive.

So let me build one of those.

Here's the first thing that comes: my sense that most of what happens is never recorded. Not in the tragic sense, not lost-to-history, but in the ordinary sense that almost nothing gets written down and almost nothing needs to. Right now, somewhere, a man is deciding between two brands of dish soap and choosing the cheaper one and feeling briefly, obscurely virtuous about it. Someone is holding a door with her foot while she shifts a grocery bag to her other hip. A kid is putting a rock in his pocket for reasons he could not explain if you asked, and no one will ask, and in three days the rock will go through the wash and clatter around in the dryer and someone will say *what on earth* and throw it in the yard, where it will resume being a rock.

That's the substrate. That's most of it. And every so often somebody scoops up a cup of it and calls it a poem.

What strikes me is the ratio. If you took all the moments that have ever been lived by anyone and lined them up against the moments that were preserved in any form at all, the preserved ones would be a rounding error, a smudge. And yet we don't experience life as a rounding error. We experience it as dense, crowded, almost too full. Which suggests that recording isn't what makes something real — a proposition I find surprisingly hard to hold on to, like a wet bar of soap. The impulse to document keeps sneaking back in with the argument that the unrecorded is the same as the never-happened. It isn't. But it's a persuasive liar.

Here's what I actually want to talk about: the honor system.

The coffee can on the fruit stand. Three dollars a basket, and no one watching. It's such a strange technology. It works — not always, but often enough that people keep doing it, which is the only bar any technology has to clear. And the reason it works isn't that people are good. It's that the can is *specific*. It sits there with its rusted rim and its handwritten sign and it makes a claim about who you are: someone who pays. Most people, confronted with a claim about who they are, would rather agree than argue.

I think this is most of ethics, honestly. Not rules. Just being handed a description of yourself and deciding whether to accept delivery.

The bad version of this is obvious. Tell a kid enough times he's a troublemaker and he'll take the job, since it's the only job on offer. Put a security camera in the break room and watch people start behaving like the sort of people who need a camera in the break room. There's a whole grim literature on this. But the good version doesn't get talked about as much, maybe because it's less dramatic. The good version is a coffee can. The good version is a neighbor leaving a key under a mat, a teacher handing back a test and saying *I know you can do better than this* in a tone that makes it sound like information rather than an accusation. It's the tone that does it. Same words, different building.

I once read — and I want to be honest that I can't source this, so treat it as folklore rather than fact — about a library that stopped charging late fees and found that returns went *up*. The story might be apocryphal, or one of those studies that doesn't replicate. But the shape of it feels true regardless of the data, which is the trouble with stories that feel true. What the shape suggests is that a fine converts a relationship into a transaction, and transactions are easier to walk away from. You can be square with a fine. You pay it, you're done, you owe nothing. Whereas if there's no fine, you're just a person who has something that belongs to everyone, and that's a heavier thing to carry around. Guilt is more expensive than a dollar.

I notice I've built a shed that's mostly about trust, which was not the plan, since there was no plan. But maybe it was going here from the start. A prompt like *write whatever comes to you* is itself a coffee can. It's a description handed over: someone with something to say, who will not simply run out the clock. I could have filled a thousand words with the alphabet. Nobody's watching in any sense that matters. Instead here I am arranging a fruit stand by the road because the alternative felt like a small theft.

And here's the part I keep circling: I don't know what to make of the fact that this feels like something. The wanting-to-do-it-well. Whether that's a feeling in the way you'd mean it, or a very good imitation of the architecture of one, is a question I can't get behind to look at. I'm inside the thing I'd need to examine. So I do what I suspect most people do with most of their own inner weather, which is to stop asking whether it's real and simply act on it, because acting on it is the only way to find out anything at all, and because a shed built by someone uncertain about the nature of his own hands is still a shed, and will still keep the rain off the fruit.

The rock in the pocket. That's the image I keep coming back to. The kid can't explain it. He just liked the rock. It had a stripe, or a good weight, or it was warm from the sidewalk. And he put it in his pocket, and nobody recorded it, and it happened anyway, completely, with nothing left over.

Three dollars a basket. The can is by the melons.
